claims.text: Service exposure induces a diffusion-controlled transformation in Mg-containing lightweight HEAs.
Mg rapidly segregates and nucleates coarse intermetallic precipitates during service exposure.
Phase separation depletes the matrix of elements that stabilize corrosion resistance and protective oxide formation.
Matrix depletion degrades corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance relative to the initial metastable solid-solution state.
The initial material is a homogeneous metastable solid solution with uniformly distributed Mg and other alloying elements.
Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates nucleate and grow both at grain boundaries and within grains.
Mg has relatively high mobility at the proposed service temperatures.
Mg segregation and clustering lower the nucleation barrier for intermetallic precipitation.
Intermetallic coprecipitation partitions other elements, including potentially corrosion- or oxidation-resistant elements, away from the contiguous matrix.
Elemental partitioning causes the protective oxide scale to become discontinuous or non-adherent.
Aged samples will contain detectable Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates relative to the as-cast state.
Aged samples will exhibit higher corrosion current densities than as-cast samples.
Aged samples will develop thicker, non-protective oxide scales or faster TGA degradation rates than as-cast samples.
Before precipitation, the initial metastable solid solution can form a coherent protective oxide layer upon exposure.
The proposed transformation occurs predominantly at 400–600 °C in oxidizing atmospheres.
Below 400 °C, diffusion is too slow to cause noticeable precipitation over the stated exposure durations.
At temperatures much higher than 600 °C, additional phases or degradation mechanisms may dominate.
